teaser.text: Hershey is a branded food company best known for chocolate, but it also sells candy, salty snacks, protein bars and ingredients. Its dollar comes in through retailers and distributors, then goes out through ingredients, factories, delivery, selling costs, financing and taxes.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Hershey's forecast, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case gives earnings of $1,525 million, $1,587 million and $1,651 million across the three dates. It assumes expensive cocoa coverage, continued price-driven volume weakness and limited productivity gains. The bull case reaches $1,991 million, $2,261 million and $2,520 million because cocoa relief arrives faster, pricing holds and Dot’s capacity and snack brands improve margins. Q2 pricing was about 12% favorable while volume/mix fell about 8%, so the forecast does not assume that price increases are costless.

The base story is a delayed but broad recovery. Guidance supports the earnings bridge, lower cocoa costs gradually improve margins, and measured buybacks preserve cash for debt and investment. Base begins at $174.49 and ends at $224.80. Its probability is 54% because earnings, shares and dividends specialists each identify recovery as the most likely path, while volume weakness reduces confidence.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Hershey really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is operating cash less capital spending. Hershey generated US$1,822,745 thousand on that simple basis in 2025, down from US$1,925,654 thousand in 2024. Deducting stock compensation produces analytical “real free cash flow” of US$1,757,285 thousand, because shares given to employees still transfer value even without an immediate cash payment.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Hershey today?

paragraphs.text: The P/E ratio shows how much investors pay for one dollar of annual earnings per share. Hershey’s trailing P/E of 22.8 implies earnings of about $7.32 per share, while its forward P/E of 16.9 implies about $9.88. The lower forward multiple does not mean the stock became cheaper; it means investors expect profit to recover.

blocks.heading: How much does Hershey pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends begin at the annualized rate of $5.81. The base case increases them to $6.10 and then $6.38, below the pace implied by a full earnings recovery. The bear case holds the payout at $6.00 after a pause, while the bull case reaches $6.24 and then $6.72. The current rate and long record of uninterrupted payments support continuity, but debt, investment and repurchases compete for cash.

Deducting stock compensation produces analytical “real free cash flow” of US$1,757,285 thousand, because shares given to employees still transfer value even without an immediate cash payment.

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after Hershey collects from customers, pays suppliers and invests in factories, equipment and software. Its 5.4% yield is only slightly above the 5.15% 10-year U.S. Treasury yield on October 19, 2026, and it is not a promised return. Cash can be tied up in cocoa and inventory before holiday sales, while planned 2026 capital spending of $425 million to $475 million limits what remains for dividends or debt repayment.

The bull case would become more credible if cocoa coverage rolls off quickly, takeaway stabilizes and Dot’s capacity and snack brands produce organic profit. The October 29, 2026 earnings release is the next dated test.

blocks.heading: What is Hershey's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: The dividend yield is 3.5%, but it comes from the same cash pool as reinvestment, so it should not be added to the free-cash-flow yield. Hershey also has two share classes: Common Stock has one vote per share, while Class B has ten. Common receives a dividend 10% higher, so the two classes offer different combinations of income and control.

earnings.title: Hershey earnings: guidance and what to watch
earnings.meta_description: Hershey reports next on October 29, 2026; see its guidance, recent results and the volume, margin and cocoa costs to watch.
earnings.opening: Hershey's next results are expected on October 29, 2026. Watch whether Hershey's volume improves as prices rise.
earnings.closing: The full memo also answers how Hershey makes money, identifies Hershey rivals, explains Hershey management, and examines Hershey risks.

paragraphs.text: On July 30, Hershey narrowed its 2026 forecast by raising the floor and leaving the ceiling unchanged. Adjusted diluted earnings per share (EPS), which measures profit per share after selected items are removed, are now expected to reach $8.36–$8.52, up 32.5%–35.0%. Guidance is management’s public forecast, not a guarantee.

Hershey expects 2026 sales growth of 4.5%–5.0%, including 150 basis points from acquiring snack business LesserEvil. Organic growth, which excludes acquisitions and currency movements, is expected to reach 3.0%–3.5%. That measure says more about Hershey’s existing products.

blocks.heading: What does Hershey's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue was US$2,787,306 thousand in June 2026, versus US$2,614,718 thousand in June 2025. It rose 6.6%. Organic constant-currency growth was 3.6%. Pricing contributed approximately 12.0%, but volume/mix declined approximately 8.0%. Elasticity describes this response: shoppers may buy smaller packs, buy less often or switch brands when prices rise.

blocks.heading: What should Hershey watchers watch in the next release?

paragraphs.text: Hershey’s next dated checkpoint is October 29, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, when it holds its third-quarter earnings call. The first question should be volume: how many products customers bought, rather than how many dollars they spent. Higher prices can raise sales while volume falls, so improving volume would provide stronger evidence of recovery.

Cocoa costs can help or hurt each batch of chocolate. The benchmark was 3.50% lower year over year on October 19, 2026, but lower cocoa costs alone would not prove better execution. The more durable evidence would be improved margins after temporary refunds disappear.
